_link.title: I can define and apply the concept of coping flexibility

options.text: The ability to adjust or change coping strategies when circumstances change
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility is the ability to adjust or change strategies when circumstances change, when the stressor evolves, or when the original strategy no longer provides relief.

options.text: Using the same coping strategy in every situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility is about changing strategies when needed, not using the same one every time.

options.text: Avoiding all coping strategies during stressful times
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves adapting strategies, not avoiding them.

options.text: The physical ability to stretch and bend during stress
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility refers to adjusting coping strategies, not physical flexibility.

toLevel2.stem: When might a person need to demonstrate coping flexibility?

options.text: When their current coping strategy is no longer providing relief
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility is needed when the original strategy stops working, when circumstances change, or when the stressor evolves.

options.text: Only when they first experience a stressor for the very first time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility is needed throughout the coping process, particularly when the strategy is no longer effective or circumstances change.

options.text: Never, because changing strategies shows weakness
options.feedback: Incorrect. Changing strategies when needed demonstrates high coping flexibility, which supports mental wellbeing.

options.text: Only during physical exercise routines
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility applies to all types of coping strategies, not just exercise.

toLevel2.stem: What does high coping flexibility support?

options.text: Both context-specific effectiveness and overall mental wellbeing
options.feedback: Correct. High coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness (matching strategies to situations) and overall mental wellbeing.

options.text: Only physical health and nothing else
options.feedback: Incorrect. High coping flexibility specifically supports context-specific effectiveness and mental wellbeing.

options.text: Avoiding all stressful situations permanently
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility is about adapting strategies, not avoiding stressors entirely.

options.text: Using only one strategy more frequently
options.feedback: Incorrect. High coping flexibility involves being able to change strategies, not using one strategy more often.

toLevel2.stem: A student normally relieves stress by playing football, but when the season ends they switch to daily jogging. What concept does this demonstrate?

options.text: Coping flexibility, because they adapted their strategy to changed circumstances
options.feedback: Correct. Switching from football to jogging when the season ends shows the ability to adjust coping strategies when circumstances change.

options.text: Poor coping, because they abandoned their original strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Changing strategies when the original is no longer available demonstrates good coping flexibility, not poor coping.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness only, with no coping flexibility involved
options.feedback: Incorrect. While context-specific effectiveness is related, the act of changing strategy in response to changed circumstances specifically demonstrates coping flexibility.

options.text: Stress avoidance, because they stopped playing football
options.feedback: Incorrect. Switching to jogging demonstrates adapting to changed circumstances, not avoiding stress.

toLevel2.stem: How does coping flexibility differ from context-specific effectiveness?

options.text: Coping flexibility is about changing strategies when conditions change, while context-specific effectiveness is about selecting the right strategy for a given situation
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility focuses on the ability to adapt and change strategies, while context-specific effectiveness focuses on matching a strategy to the current demands.

options.text: They are the same concept with different names
options.feedback: Incorrect. They are distinct concepts. Coping flexibility is about adapting, while context-specific effectiveness is about selecting the right strategy for the situation.

options.text: Coping flexibility is about choosing the first strategy and never changing it
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility is specifically about the ability to change strategies when needed.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness means always using the same approach
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means matching the strategy to the situation's demands, which may require different strategies for different situations.

toLevel2.stem: Coping flexibility involves adjusting or changing strategies when the initial strategy is no longer providing relief.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility is the ability to adjust or change strategies when circumstances change or the original strategy no longer works.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility does involve adjusting strategies when they are no longer effective or when circumstances change.

toLevel2.stem: High coping flexibility means sticking to the same strategy regardless of whether it is working.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Incorrect. High coping flexibility means being able to change strategies when needed, not rigidly sticking to one that is no longer working.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. High coping flexibility involves the ability to adjust or change strategies when circumstances change or the current strategy is no longer effective.

toLevel2.stem: Coping flexibility is the ability to {{blank:1}} or change coping strategies when {{blank:2}} change.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves adjusting strategies, not abandoning coping altogether.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility means adjusting strategies in response to changing circumstances, not ignoring changes.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility is needed when circumstances change, not when nothing changes.
Incorrect. While environment can be a factor, the broader concept is that coping flexibility responds to changing circumstances.

toLevel2.stem: High coping flexibility supports both context-specific {{blank:1}} and overall mental {{blank:2}}.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. High coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness, not context-specific avoidance.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness, helping people match strategies to situations.
Incorrect. High coping flexibility supports mental wellbeing, not mental illness.
Incorrect. High coping flexibility supports mental wellbeing, not fatigue.

toLevel2.stem: When a student switches from football to jogging after the season ends, they are demonstrating coping {{blank:1}} by adapting to {{blank:2}} circumstances.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Switching strategies shows flexibility, not rigidity. Rigidity would mean sticking to football even when it is unavailable.
Incorrect. Switching to jogging is an adaptation, not avoidance of coping.
Incorrect. The circumstances have changed (football season ended), which is why the student adapted their strategy.
Incorrect. The circumstances changed when the football season ended, prompting the switch to jogging.

toLevel3.stem: Why is coping flexibility considered a distinct concept from context-specific effectiveness in VCE Psychology?

options.text: Because coping flexibility focuses on the ability to change strategies over time, while context-specific effectiveness focuses on choosing the right strategy for a given moment
options.feedback: Correct. They address different aspects of coping: flexibility is about adapting over time, while context-specific effectiveness is about matching strategy to current demands.

options.text: Because they are actually the same concept and should not be distinguished
options.feedback: Incorrect. They are explicitly distinct concepts in VCE Psychology, each assessed separately.

options.text: Because coping flexibility only applies to physical strategies like exercise
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility applies to all types of coping strategies, not just physical ones.

options.text: Because context-specific effectiveness is not part of the VCE curriculum
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both concepts are part of the VCE curriculum and are assessed as distinct concepts.

toLevel3.stem: How does high coping flexibility contribute to mental wellbeing?

options.text: It allows a person to adapt their strategies when circumstances change, ensuring they continue to cope effectively rather than being stuck with an ineffective approach
options.feedback: Correct. By adapting strategies, a person maintains effective coping as circumstances evolve, supporting ongoing mental wellbeing.

options.text: It prevents a person from ever experiencing stress in the first place
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility helps manage stress more effectively, not prevent it entirely.

options.text: It means a person never needs to use any coping strategies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves using and adapting strategies, not avoiding them.

options.text: It guarantees perfect mental health regardless of stressor severity
options.feedback: Incorrect. While high coping flexibility supports wellbeing, it does not guarantee perfect mental health.

toLevel3.stem: A person has been using deep breathing to manage work stress, but recently it is no longer helping because the stressor has become more severe. What would demonstrate coping flexibility?

options.text: Recognising that deep breathing is no longer sufficient and switching to or adding a different strategy
options.feedback: Correct. Recognising that the current strategy is ineffective and changing approach demonstrates coping flexibility.

options.text: Continuing to use deep breathing with greater intensity
options.feedback: Incorrect. Persisting with an ineffective strategy does not demonstrate coping flexibility. Adjusting the approach would.

options.text: Giving up on coping entirely because one strategy failed
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves switching strategies, not abandoning coping altogether.

options.text: Blaming the deep breathing technique for being a bad strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Deep breathing may have been effective initially. The issue is that circumstances changed and the strategy needs to be adapted.

toLevel3.stem: How can you identify coping flexibility in a scenario?

options.text: Look for a person changing their coping approach in response to changing demands or when the original strategy stops working
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility is identified when a person adjusts or changes their strategy because circumstances have changed or the original strategy is no longer effective.

options.text: Look for a person who never changes their strategy under any circumstances
options.feedback: Incorrect. Never changing strategy indicates low coping flexibility, not high.

options.text: Look for a person who avoids all stressors completely
options.feedback: Incorrect. Avoiding stressors entirely does not demonstrate coping flexibility, which is about adapting strategies.

options.text: Look for a person who only uses one type of coping strategy throughout their life
options.feedback: Incorrect. Using only one strategy shows low coping flexibility. High flexibility involves adapting strategies to changing circumstances.

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between coping flexibility and context-specific effectiveness?

options.text: Coping flexibility enables context-specific effectiveness by allowing a person to change strategies as situations change
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness because the ability to change strategies ensures the person can always select a strategy appropriate to the current demands.

options.text: They are opposites — coping flexibility undermines context-specific effectiveness
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness by enabling strategy changes when demands shift.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness eliminates the need for coping flexibility
options.feedback: Incorrect. Even with context-specific effectiveness, circumstances change over time, requiring coping flexibility to maintain effective coping.

options.text: They have no relationship to each other
options.feedback: Incorrect. They are related — high coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness by allowing adaptation to changing circumstances.

toLevel3.stem: A student explains: 'Coping flexibility means you should change your strategy every day to be effective.' What is wrong with this explanation?

options.text: Coping flexibility means changing when circumstances change or the strategy stops working, not changing arbitrarily every day
options.feedback: Correct. Changing strategy should be in response to changed demands or ineffective coping, not arbitrary daily changes.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — daily changes are exactly what coping flexibility requires
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility responds to changed circumstances, not a fixed schedule of daily changes.

options.text: Coping flexibility means never changing your strategy at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility does involve changing strategies, but in response to changing demands, not never.

options.text: Changing strategies is always harmful regardless of the reason
options.feedback: Incorrect. Changing strategies in response to changed circumstances is beneficial and demonstrates high coping flexibility.

toLevel3.stem: Coping flexibility is directly assessed as a distinct concept in VCE Psychology.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Coping flexibility is a distinct concept from context-specific effectiveness and is directly assessed in VCE Psychology.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility is indeed directly assessed as a distinct concept in VCE Psychology.

toLevel3.stem: Coping flexibility enables context-specific {{blank:1}} by allowing a person to {{blank:2}} strategies as situations change.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility supports context-specific effectiveness, not avoidance.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility supports effectiveness, not failure, by enabling strategy adaptation.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves changing strategies, not avoiding them.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves changing to new strategies, not repeating the same one.

toLevel3.stem: A person demonstrating low coping flexibility would {{blank:1}} with an ineffective strategy despite changed {{blank:2}}.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Adapting would demonstrate high flexibility. Persisting with an ineffective strategy shows low flexibility.
Incorrect. Experimenting with new strategies would show flexibility. Low flexibility involves persisting with what is not working.
Incorrect. The scenario describes changed circumstances, not unchanged ones.
Incorrect. While weather could be one circumstance, the broader concept is changed circumstances generally.

toLevel3.stem: To identify coping flexibility in a scenario, look for someone {{blank:1}} their approach when the original strategy is no longer providing {{blank:2}}.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Maintaining the same approach when it is not working shows low coping flexibility. Look for someone changing their approach.
Incorrect. Ignoring the need to adapt is not coping flexibility. Look for someone actively changing their approach.
Incorrect. The strategy should be changed when it no longer provides relief, not when it no longer provides stress.
Incorrect. The trigger for changing strategy is when it no longer provides relief from stress.

toLevel4.stem: Li has been managing exam stress by studying with friends. Her study group disbands because members move away. Li continues to try organising group study sessions despite having no available group members. What does this demonstrate about her coping flexibility?

options.text: Low coping flexibility, because she persists with a strategy that can no longer work given the changed circumstances
options.feedback: Correct. Li's circumstances have changed (no available group members), but she has not adapted her strategy, showing low coping flexibility.

options.text: High coping flexibility, because she is persistent and determined
options.feedback: Incorrect. Persistence with an ineffective strategy shows low flexibility, not high. High flexibility would involve adapting to the new circumstances.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness, because group study is always the best strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Group study is no longer possible given Li's circumstances. Continuing this strategy is not context-specifically effective.

options.text: No relevance to coping flexibility because studying is not a coping strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Studying with friends was Li's coping strategy for exam stress, and her inability to adapt shows low coping flexibility.

toLevel4.stem: Max initially copes with work stress by going to the gym, but after injuring his knee, he switches to meditation and journaling. Apply the concept of coping flexibility to explain Max's behaviour.

options.text: Max demonstrates high coping flexibility by recognising his original strategy is no longer viable and switching to alternatives that suit his changed circumstances
options.feedback: Correct. Max adapted his coping approach when his injury made gym-going impossible, demonstrating coping flexibility by choosing strategies that match his current circumstances.

options.text: Max shows low coping flexibility because he gave up on exercise
options.feedback: Incorrect. Max adapted to his injury by switching strategies, which shows high, not low, coping flexibility.

options.text: Max should have continued going to the gym despite the injury
options.feedback: Incorrect. Persisting with a strategy that is no longer viable (due to injury) would show low coping flexibility. Switching demonstrates adaptability.

options.text: Max's behaviour has no connection to coping flexibility
options.feedback: Incorrect. Switching strategies in response to changed circumstances (injury) is a direct example of coping flexibility.

toLevel4.stem: A VCE exam presents a scenario where a student switches from avoidance strategies to approach strategies after their stressor becomes controllable. What concept is the exam most likely assessing?

options.text: Coping flexibility, because the student changed their strategy in response to changing demands
options.feedback: Correct. Switching strategy type when the nature of the stressor changes (from uncontrollable to controllable) directly demonstrates coping flexibility.

options.text: Only context-specific effectiveness, with no relevance to coping flexibility
options.feedback: Incorrect. While context-specific effectiveness is related, the act of switching strategies in response to changing demands is specifically coping flexibility.

options.text: The fight-or-flight response, because the student is choosing how to react physically
options.feedback: Incorrect. This scenario is about coping strategies, not the fight-or-flight response.

options.text: The GAS model, because all coping involves physiological adaptation
options.feedback: Incorrect. This scenario assesses coping flexibility in strategy selection, not the GAS model's physiological stages.

toLevel4.stem: Sarah uses distraction to cope with anxiety about a medical test result she cannot change. When the results arrive and reveal a treatable condition, she switches to making a treatment plan. How does coping flexibility explain this transition?

options.text: Sarah adapted her strategy from avoidance (distraction while waiting) to approach (planning treatment) when the situation changed, demonstrating coping flexibility
options.feedback: Correct. Sarah changed strategies when her circumstances changed — from an uncontrollable wait to a treatable condition — showing coping flexibility.

options.text: Sarah showed low coping flexibility because she used two different strategies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Using different strategies in response to changed circumstances demonstrates high, not low, coping flexibility.

options.text: Sarah should have used the same strategy throughout because changing strategies is ineffective
options.feedback: Incorrect. Changing strategies when circumstances change is effective and demonstrates high coping flexibility.

options.text: This example is unrelated to coping flexibility because medical situations do not count
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility applies to all stressful situations, including medical ones.

toLevel4.stem: Two employees face redundancy. Employee A tries one strategy (updating their resume) and when it does not immediately relieve stress, gives up coping entirely. Employee B tries updating their resume, then adds networking and mindfulness when the stress persists. Which employee demonstrates higher coping flexibility?

options.text: Employee B, because they added new strategies when the initial one was insufficient, adapting their approach to ongoing demands
options.feedback: Correct. Employee B adjusted their approach by adding strategies when the initial one was not enough, demonstrating high coping flexibility.

options.text: Employee A, because they recognised quickly that coping does not work
options.feedback: Incorrect. Giving up entirely shows low coping flexibility. Recognising a strategy is insufficient should lead to trying alternatives.

options.text: Both show equal coping flexibility because both tried updating their resume
options.feedback: Incorrect. The difference is in their response when the initial strategy was insufficient. Employee B adapted while Employee A gave up.

options.text: Neither shows coping flexibility because job loss cannot be coped with
options.feedback: Incorrect. Job loss is a stressor that can be managed through coping strategies. Employee B demonstrates coping flexibility by adapting their approach.

toLevel4.stem: A student writes in an exam: 'The person should use approach strategies because approach strategies are always better.' The scenario describes a bereavement where the person has already changed from approach to avoidance strategies. How could the student improve their answer using coping flexibility?

options.text: By acknowledging that switching to avoidance demonstrates coping flexibility because the person adapted to the emotional demands of bereavement
options.feedback: Correct. Recognising that the switch itself demonstrates coping flexibility, and that avoidance may be appropriate for the emotional demands of bereavement, shows deeper understanding.

options.text: By insisting more strongly that approach is always better
options.feedback: Incorrect. Making a general claim ignores coping flexibility and context-specific effectiveness. The switch to avoidance may be appropriate for bereavement.

options.text: By removing all mention of coping strategies from their answer
options.feedback: Incorrect. The answer should engage with coping flexibility to explain why the person changed strategies.

options.text: By stating that bereavement does not require any coping
options.feedback: Incorrect. Bereavement is a significant stressor that benefits from coping strategies, and the person's strategy switch demonstrates coping flexibility.

toLevel4.stem: How would a person with low coping flexibility likely respond to a stressor that changes significantly over time?

options.text: They would continue using the same strategy even as it becomes less effective for the evolving stressor
options.feedback: Correct. Low coping flexibility means the person struggles to adapt their approach, persisting with a strategy that may no longer match the demands.

options.text: They would immediately switch to the most effective strategy for every change
options.feedback: Incorrect. Immediately switching to the best strategy for each change would demonstrate high, not low, coping flexibility.

options.text: They would try multiple strategies simultaneously from the start
options.feedback: Incorrect. Low coping flexibility is characterised by inability to change strategies, not by trying many at once.

options.text: They would have no stress response at all because low flexibility means low stress
options.feedback: Incorrect. Low coping flexibility does not mean low stress. It means difficulty adapting strategies, which may worsen stress over time.

toLevel4.stem: Li's persistence with group study despite having no available members demonstrates {{blank:1}} coping flexibility because she has not {{blank:2}} her strategy to her changed circumstances.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Persisting with an impossible strategy shows low, not high, coping flexibility.
Incorrect. Failing to change strategy when it is clearly no longer possible indicates low coping flexibility.
Incorrect. The issue is not abandoning coping but adapting the strategy to changed circumstances.
Incorrect. Li is repeating the same approach. The issue is that she has not adapted to the new situation.

toLevel4.stem: Max switching from gym to meditation after his injury demonstrates {{blank:1}} coping flexibility because he adapted to {{blank:2}} circumstances.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Adapting strategies in response to changed circumstances demonstrates high, not low, coping flexibility.
Incorrect. Max clearly demonstrates coping flexibility by switching strategies after his injury.
Incorrect. Max's circumstances changed — he was injured and could no longer go to the gym.
Incorrect. The injury changed Max's circumstances, prompting him to adapt his coping strategy.

toLevel4.stem: Sarah switching from {{blank:1}} while waiting for results to making a treatment {{blank:2}} when the condition was treatable demonstrates coping flexibility.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Sarah used distraction while waiting for results and then switched to planning when the situation changed.
Incorrect. Sarah used distraction (an avoidance strategy) while waiting, not confrontation.
Incorrect. Sarah switched from avoidance (distraction) to approach (making a treatment plan) when the situation changed.
Incorrect. Sarah made a treatment plan (approach strategy), not engaged in denial, when the results arrived.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the claim: 'A person with high coping flexibility will always experience lower stress than someone with low coping flexibility.'

options.text: This overstates the benefit — high flexibility supports better coping but does not guarantee lower stress, as stress depends on many factors including stressor severity and available resources
options.feedback: Correct. While high coping flexibility supports effective coping, stress levels are influenced by many factors. A severe stressor may cause significant stress even for someone with high coping flexibility.

options.text: This is entirely correct because coping flexibility eliminates all stress
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility helps manage stress but does not eliminate it. Stress depends on many factors beyond coping flexibility alone.

options.text: This is entirely incorrect because coping flexibility has no effect on stress
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility does support stress management. The issue is that it does not guarantee lower stress in all situations.

options.text: This is correct because flexibility is the only factor that determines stress levels
options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiple factors influence stress levels including stressor severity, resources, and support systems. Flexibility is one important factor but not the only one.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how coping flexibility and context-specific effectiveness work together to support mental wellbeing. Why are both concepts necessary?

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness ensures the right strategy is chosen initially, and coping flexibility ensures the strategy is adapted when circumstances change — both are needed for sustained effective coping
options.feedback: Correct. Without context-specific effectiveness, initial strategy selection may be poor. Without coping flexibility, a person cannot adapt when circumstances evolve. Together they support ongoing effective coping.

options.text: Only one concept is necessary because they do the same thing
options.feedback: Incorrect. They address different aspects of coping — initial selection versus ongoing adaptation. Both are necessary for comprehensive stress management.

options.text: Neither is necessary because mental wellbeing is determined entirely by genetics
options.feedback: Incorrect. While genetics play a role, coping strategies significantly influence mental wellbeing, and both concepts contribute to effective coping.

options.text: Coping flexibility makes context-specific effectiveness unnecessary because flexible people do not need to choose the right strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Even flexible people benefit from initially choosing appropriate strategies. Context-specific effectiveness guides initial selection, and flexibility enables adaptation.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher argues that coping flexibility is more important than context-specific effectiveness for long-term mental wellbeing. Evaluate this argument.

options.text: Both are important — flexibility helps with long-term adaptation, but without context-specific effectiveness, the new strategies chosen may still be inappropriate
options.feedback: Correct. Flexibility enables strategy changes, but context-specific effectiveness ensures the chosen strategies are appropriate. Ranking one as more important oversimplifies their complementary roles.

options.text: The argument is correct because only flexibility matters in the long term
options.feedback: Incorrect. In the long term, both flexibility (adapting strategies) and context-specific effectiveness (choosing appropriate ones) matter.

options.text: The argument is incorrect because context-specific effectiveness is always more important
options.feedback: Incorrect. Neither concept is always more important. They serve complementary functions in effective coping.

options.text: The argument is irrelevant because neither concept affects mental wellbeing
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both coping flexibility and context-specific effectiveness are linked to mental wellbeing through effective stress management.

toLevel5.stem: Critically evaluate how a school wellbeing program could use the concept of coping flexibility to help students manage stress more effectively.

options.text: By teaching students multiple strategies and helping them recognise when their current strategy is not working so they can switch to a more appropriate one
options.feedback: Correct. An effective program would build students' repertoire of strategies and develop their ability to recognise when change is needed, supporting high coping flexibility.

options.text: By teaching students only one strategy and ensuring they use it for every stressor
options.feedback: Incorrect. Teaching only one strategy would produce low coping flexibility. Students need multiple strategies and the ability to switch between them.

options.text: By discouraging students from ever changing their coping approach
options.feedback: Incorrect. Discouraging strategy changes would reduce coping flexibility. Programs should encourage adaptive strategy switching.

options.text: By eliminating all stressors from the school environment so coping is unnecessary
options.feedback: Incorrect. Eliminating all stressors is impractical and would not prepare students for life. Building coping flexibility is more valuable.

toLevel5.stem: Compare a person who rigidly applies the same coping strategy regardless of circumstances with a person who frequently changes strategies for no clear reason. Which demonstrates appropriate coping flexibility?

options.text: Neither — appropriate coping flexibility involves changing strategies in response to changed demands, not rigidly persisting or changing randomly
options.feedback: Correct. Appropriate coping flexibility is purposeful adaptation to changed circumstances. Both rigid persistence and random changing fail to match strategy to demands.

options.text: The rigid person demonstrates better flexibility because consistency is key
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rigid persistence with one strategy shows low coping flexibility, not appropriate flexibility.

options.text: The frequently changing person demonstrates better flexibility because more changes equal more flexibility
options.feedback: Incorrect. Changing for no clear reason is not purposeful adaptation. Coping flexibility involves changing in response to changed demands or ineffective coping.

options.text: Both demonstrate equally appropriate coping flexibility
options.feedback: Incorrect. Neither demonstrates appropriate coping flexibility. Rigid persistence is too inflexible, and random changing is not purposeful.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether low coping flexibility could contribute to the exhaustion stage of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome.

options.text: Yes — if a person cannot adapt their coping strategies as the stressor persists, their resources may deplete faster, potentially contributing to exhaustion
options.feedback: Correct. Low coping flexibility means persisting with ineffective strategies, which could waste resources and leave the person unable to cope, contributing to the exhaustion stage of GAS.

options.text: No — GAS is purely biological and coping flexibility is irrelevant
options.feedback: Incorrect. While GAS is a biological model, coping strategies influence how effectively a person manages stress, potentially affecting progression through GAS stages.

options.text: No — coping flexibility only affects the alarm stage of GAS
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility affects how a person manages stress throughout all stages, potentially influencing whether exhaustion is reached.

options.text: Yes — but only because coping flexibility directly causes cortisol release
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping flexibility does not directly cause cortisol release. It affects exhaustion by influencing how effectively stress is managed.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how coping flexibility relates to Lazarus and Folkman's concept of reappraisal. How do these concepts interact?

options.text: Reappraisal involves re-evaluating the stressor and coping resources, which may lead to recognising the need to change strategy — directly triggering coping flexibility
options.feedback: Correct. When a person reappraises their situation and recognises their current strategy is ineffective, they use coping flexibility to switch to a more appropriate approach.

options.text: They are unrelated because L&F's model does not involve coping strategies
options.feedback: Incorrect. L&F's model includes coping strategies as part of the response to appraisal. Reappraisal and coping flexibility are closely related.

options.text: Reappraisal prevents the need for coping flexibility entirely
options.feedback: Incorrect. Reappraisal may actually trigger coping flexibility by revealing that the current strategy needs to change.

options.text: Coping flexibility replaces reappraisal in L&F's model
options.feedback: Incorrect. They are complementary processes. Reappraisal evaluates the situation, and coping flexibility enables strategy change based on that evaluation.

toLevel5.stem: A student writes: 'Coping flexibility is always positive because changing strategies shows adaptability.' Evaluate whether this is always true.

options.text: Not always — changing strategies without purpose or before giving a strategy enough time to work could be counterproductive rather than adaptive
options.feedback: Correct. While coping flexibility is generally positive, changing strategies too quickly or without clear reason may prevent any strategy from being effective. Purposeful adaptation is key.

options.text: Yes, any strategy change is always beneficial regardless of reason
options.feedback: Incorrect. Changing strategies needs to be purposeful and in response to changed circumstances. Random or premature changes can be counterproductive.

options.text: No, changing strategies is always negative because it shows indecisiveness
options.feedback: Incorrect. Purposeful strategy changes in response to changed circumstances demonstrate adaptive coping, not indecisiveness.

options.text: Yes, because the VCE study design says flexibility is always good
options.feedback: Incorrect. While flexibility is generally positive, it should be purposeful. Changing strategies without reason is not what coping flexibility means.

toLevel5.stem: Appropriate coping flexibility involves {{blank:1}} adaptation to changed demands, not rigid persistence or {{blank:2}} changing.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Appropriate coping flexibility is purposeful, not random. Changes should respond to evolving demands.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility does not mean constant change. It means purposeful adaptation when circumstances require it.
Incorrect. Purposeful changing is appropriate. Random changing without clear reason is not appropriate coping flexibility.
Incorrect. Effective changes are desirable. Random or purposeless changes are what should be avoided.

toLevel5.stem: Context-specific effectiveness guides initial strategy {{blank:1}}, while coping flexibility ensures the strategy is {{blank:2}} when circumstances evolve.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness guides strategy selection (choosing the right one), not strategy avoidance.
Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness is about selecting appropriate strategies, not rejecting them.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility ensures strategies are adapted when circumstances change, not rigidly maintained.
Incorrect. Coping flexibility involves adapting strategies, not abandoning coping altogether.
